name: Merck stitch otoplasty

lead: The Merck stitch is a closed, minimally invasive ear-pinning method. Sutures are placed through small puncture incisions instead of an open cut behind the ear, reshaping the ear without cutting cartilage so it sits closer to the head.

It was published in 2013 and sits within the suture-only group of otoplasty techniques, contrasted with Mustardé's open approach and larger incision. Sources describing it are sparse and no technique-specific studies were found.

paras: A surgeon passes sutures through stab incisions to fold and hold the cartilage in its new shape. Because it is closed, there is no long incision behind the ear.
General suture-otoplasty risks include suture extrusion, hematoma, infection and recurrence. No technique-specific figures were found.

angle.text: Stitches placed through tiny stab incisions reshape the ear without a long cut or cartilage cutting, setting it closer to the head. The pinned-back ear is visible after healing. It was published in 2013, and outcome data are sparse.

lead: The Merck stitch is a closed, minimally invasive otoplasty method in which sutures are placed through small stab incisions to reshape the ear without cutting the cartilage. Wikipedia dates its publication to 2013.[1]

It falls within the suture-only (cartilage-intact) group of otoplasty techniques and is contrasted with Mustardé's open approach, which uses a larger incision.[1] Published sources reviewed here give limited detail, and no clinical studies were found.

paras: Wikipedia describes the Merck method as closed and minimally invasive, using small stab incisions and leaving the cartilage intact, in contrast to Mustardé's open approach with mattress sutures and skin excision.[1] The broader literature on otoplasty complications lists suture extrusion as the most common problem with suture-based approaches.[1]

timeline.event: Merck publishes the closed stitch method.[1]
